rejected.title: The May Fourth Movement
card: New Culture Movement

from about 1915, writers and teachers such as Chen Duxiu attacked old Confucian customs and called for science, democracy and a new way of thinking. Its ideas were spread by magazines such as New Youth.

China had joined the Allies in the First World War. The Treaty of Versailles gave German rights in Shandong to Japan, not back to China. Students in Beijing protested, and the anger spread to other cities.
The protests made nationalism, the wish to see China strong and free of foreign control, a mass cause. Many people came to see the old ideas and the weak government as a reason for China's loss.

Many young Chinese now looked abroad for answers. Some turned to Marxism, and the Russian Revolution of 1917 made it seem a real option. Chen Duxiu and Li Dazhao were among the founders of the Chinese Communist Party in 1921.
rejected.remember: The 1919 anger at Versailles and the New Culture Movement's new ideas led some young Chinese to communism.

a.q: Why did the Treaty of Versailles cause protests in China in 1919?
opts: It handed Germany's rights in Shandong to Japan
It let Germany keep its rights in Shandong
It returned Shandong to China under Allied control
It treated China as a defeated ally of Germany
a.why: China had fought on the Allied side and expected Germany's rights in Shandong to come back to it, but the treaty gave them to Japan. Letting Germany keep them is a near miss: Germany lost the rights, but China still did not get them.
a.clue: China was on the winning side. What did it expect to gain?

b.q: Lin is a Beijing student in 1920. She reads New Youth and has joined a study group on Marxism. Which best explains why she is drawn to new ideas?
opts: Versailles and New Culture ideas turned her from old ways
The Communist Party had recruited her to its study group
New Culture writers urged her to revive Confucian values
Versailles had raised her trust in the Republic's leaders
b.why: The anger at Versailles and the New Culture Movement's attack on old customs led many young people to look abroad for answers, including Marxism. The Communist Party is tempting, but it was not founded until 1921, so in 1920 it could not have recruited her.
b.clue: Think about what made young people lose faith in old answers.

a.q: Why did the Treaty of Versailles cause protests in China in 1919?
opts: It gave German rights in Shandong to Japan, not to China
It forced China to pay war costs to Germany
It made China a colony of the Allied powers
It ended Qing rule and began the Republic
a.why: China had been on the winning side, yet Shandong went to Japan. This angered students and fed nationalism. The Qing fell in 1912, years before the treaty, so the treaty did not end their rule.
a.clue: Think about who got the German rights in Shandong.

b.q: Lin is a Beijing student in 1920. She reads New Youth and has joined a study group on Marxism. Which best explains why she is drawn to new ideas?
opts: Anger at Versailles and new ideas made her doubt old ways
The Qing court ordered students to study Marxist writings
Peasants in her village had asked her to lead them in revolt
The Republic's government had made communism its policy
b.why: The May Fourth protests and the New Culture Movement led many young people to doubt old customs and look for new answers, including Marxism. The other options are not supported: the Republic's government did not adopt communism, and the Qing had already fallen.
b.clue: Which option links the 1919 protests with the new magazines?

a.best: It gave German rights in Shandong to Japan, not to China

b.best: Anger at Versailles and new ideas made her doubt old ways

problems.detail: The clue 'Think about who got the German rights in Shandong' gives the answer away. Only one option mentions Shandong, so a student can match the words without knowing the idea.
The clue 'Which option links the 1919 protests with the new magazines?' points straight at the only option that mentions Versailles and new ideas, which gives the answer away.

The distractors are implausible for Year 12. A Qing court ordering study in 1920, peasants asking a Beijing student to lead a revolt, and a Republic adopting communism can all be ruled out without any knowledge of the May Fourth Movement.
